title: How to Configure Your VPN to Work at the Router Level (and Why You Should)
description: Secure every device on your network from a single point of entry.
fullText:
When you install a VPN on a device, it’s like locking the door to a single room in your house. That room may be safe from intruders, but the rest of the house stays open and exposed. Going with that analogy, VPNs that work directly from your router lock down your front gate. They protect the entire house, with all the rooms and safes in it. By configuring your VPN at the router level, you are forcing all connected devices in your network to go through the encrypted tunnel created by your VPN. That means any devices that don't natively support VPN apps, like your smart TV or PS5, are also covered by the same level of network security.

That said, there are caveats. For example, some users have claimed that Xbox has banned them for using VPNs, though I have found no official source to confirm this at the time. Some banking platforms and financial apps may even refuse access to VPN traffic, forcing you to use a separate network for those tasks. With that in mind, I’m going to walk you through the pros and cons of setting up a VPN on your router, along with instructions on how to do it depending on your router model.

Enabling a VPN through an app on your device creates a TCP tunnel that routes your traffic through a remote server, which encrypts all traffic going in and out of that specific device. If a provider or website tries to trace that traffic back to its originating IP address, they’re pointed to the remote server instead of your local network. But this only works for the device that has a VPN enabled, while all the other traffic moving through your home network is still unencrypted and exposed. Configuring your VPN connection for every device on the network can take a lot of effort, which can lead to slip-ups that expose your online activity unintentionally.

Many advanced wifi routers come with built-in firmware support for secure communication protocols like OpenVPN, WireGuard, PPTP, and L2TP Over IPsec. This makes it possible for you to set up your VPN directly on your router, so that every device on your network stays within the encrypted tunnel all of the time, unless you disable it. You enable the VPN through the router’s own firmware, usually through a dedicated settings page that lets you enter your VPN server and credentials.

There are many benefits to this method. When you configure your VPN on a single router instead of ten different devices with their own separate apps, firmware updates and security patches are much easier to install. Many routers also offer a kill switch that will automatically block all internet traffic if your VPN is somehow disconnected, which adds another layer of protection from sudden exposure.

That said, there are some caveats that come with this arrangement. You should be aware of them now so you can plan ahead before you continue with this setup. Installing a VPN on your router means creating a single point of failure for your home network’s encryption tunnel. Hackers who successfully breach your router’s firmware can disable your VPN across every device, a common attack pattern that targets older router models. While traffic between your router and the internet goes through the VPN tunnel, any traffic passing between your local devices and the router is still unencrypted and exposed to anyone who has access to your home network.

As previously mentioned, certain platforms, like banking apps and streaming services, may automatically block VPN traffic to comply with local security, privacy, or IP protection laws. When accessing these services, you’ll have to disable your VPN at the router level, which may also leave other devices exposed. In addition, advanced features like cookie blockers, split tunneling, or post-quantum encryption (PQE) may only be accessible through a provider’s VPN apps, which won’t be available if you configure it through your router’s firmware.

Finally, since your router’s processor now handles the TCP encryption, a weak router with a suboptimal processor can cause performance issues across your entire network. You shouldn’t experience issues with more powerful router models like the ASUS RT-BE58U or Synology RT6600ax, but these can cost anywhere between $100 and $350, or even more.

First, you must confirm that your wifi router model supports VPN protocols. Look for any mention of OpenVPN or WireGuard protocol support in the router’s product documentation. Many popular VPN providers like Surfshark, ExpressVPN, and Nord VPN will also maintain a list of supported router models on their own websites, with step-by-step instructions for configuration. While individual steps can vary quite a bit depending on your router’s make and model, firmware version, and VPN protocol, some things remain similar across manufacturers and vendors:

ASUS makes it as painless as possible to get a VPN working on their routers, though not all models support all vendors and protocols. You can usually double-check with your VPN’s documentation to see if your existing model is supported. After you confirm support, here are the steps to actually get it working:

On a device connected to your router’s wifi, access the ASUS Router WebGUI and make sure that your firmware is updated to at least version 3.0.0.4.388.23000. You can also use the ASUS Router mobile app on your phone if you prefer.

Navigate to VPN, then VPN Fusion.

In the VPN Fusion tab, click Add profile and set your VPN type or provider, such as OpenVPN, WireGuard, PPTP, or L2TP.

From here, you can upload your VPN’s configuration file or manually enter the VPN service’s IP address and Port. Once done, make sure to toggle on Apply to all devices and click Apply all settings to save.

Enabling the profile you just created in the VPN Fusion tab will automatically connect your router to the VPN server.

On GL.iNET routers running a 4.x firmware version, you can access a VPN client directly from your router’s admin GUI. These routers support all OpenVPN and WireGuard-based VPN services.

Download your VPN configuration file (WireGuard or OpenVPN) from your provider’s website.

Sign into your GL.iNET router’s admin panel, then navigate to VPN > VPN Client Profile.

Click on Add Manually to upload your VPN configuration file.

Once configured, VPN protection is extended to all devices on the network by default. To enable or disable VPN on specific devices, you can use the VPN Dashboard. From here, you can also choose which VPN server your router connects to and set rule-based exceptions to bypass the VPN when accessing certain whitelisted IP addresses.

After finishing, remember to click Apply on the VPN Dashboard.

Not every TP-Link router supports VPN configuration, while even fewer support VPNs that use the WireGuard protocol. That said, if you’re on the Archer BE, GE, AX, AXE, GX, MR, or TL-MR models, you’ll find a VPN client baked into the online GUI. Here’s how to set it up:

While connected to your TP-Link router, go to tplinkwifi.net.

From there, navigate to Advanced > VPN Client. Enable the VPN Client toggle and click Save.

Under the Server List section of the VPN Client tab, click Add and choose your VPN type.

TP-Link routers support up to six VPN profiles and WireGuard, OpenVPN, PPTP, as well as L2TP/IPSec protocols. You can upload your VPN configuration file directly to create a new profile. Then enable it by flipping on the toggle next to the profile.

Unlike other router manufacturers, TP-Link does not enable VPN on all connected devices by default. You must manually enable VPN connections per device by enabling them under the VPN Device List.

Beyond the manufacturers we just covered, there are plenty of other router models that support VPNs. While default VPN support on different router models can be a mixed bag, you can also flash custom firmware on your router to enable support. However, note that improperly flashing custom firmware on your router can render it unusable. If you intend to go this route, be sure to follow your VPN provider’s official documentation for the specific steps for your router. For example, Proton VPN has published router-specific flashing guides for different manufacturers and model numbers.

If you don’t want to go through the trouble of uploading configuration files or flashing firmware, many router models now ship with pre-configured VPN support for popular services like ExpressVPN or Nord.

ExpressVPN Fortify: Layered on top of GL.iNet's Flint 2 hardware, ExpressVPN Fortify is a pre-configured VPN router that launched this September. It costs $199.99 and comes with 12 months of ExpressVPN Advanced. This router model can support 86 concurrent devices and speeds of up to 900 Mbps on WireGuard.

FlashRouters: FlashRouters sells various router models with its own open-source VPN firmware pre-configured on arrival. You can choose from ASUS, GL.iNet, and TP-Link models. But if you would rather keep your existing router, FlashRouters also offers a “Flash My Router” service for your existing hardware.

Cudy Mesh: Cudy’s mesh-ready router models like the WR5000 or WR3600 ship with a native Surfshark integration built into the Cudy App or GUI. If you 

Once you have your VPN up and running on the router, don’t assume that it works by default. Connect a device to your router’s wifi network and visit an IP detection tool like DNS Checker, What Is My IP Address, or BrowserLeaks to verify that your real IP address isn’t exposed with the VPN enabled.

If your router comes with a VPN kill switch, you should test that too. Disconnect the VPN, then try to access any website using your web browser while connected to the router’s network. If internet access is immediately disabled, the kill switch is working.

title: ICE officer who shot Venezuelan man wasn't wearing a body camera, sources say
description:
The Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who shot a Venezuelan delivery driver in Austin, Texas, on Sunday was not wearing a body camera at the time of the shooting, sources familiar with the investigation told CBS News.
An ICE officer shot Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old native of Venezuela who federal officials said has a deportation order, in the upper torso on Sunday afternoon while Garces Perez was working for DoorDash, according to local authorities and his attorney.
The shooting was the latest involving federal agents enforcing President Trump's crackdown on illegal immigration and has sparked protests in Texas, as well as calls for accountability and a transparent, independent investigation.
The lack of body camera footage from the ICE officer who shot Garces Perez — a detail first reported by The Atlantic —  is likely to escalate concerns about the shooting.

title: 10 'Homebrew' Hacks Every Mac Power User Should Know
description: Homebrew, the best package manager for Mac, just got better.
fullText:
Homebrew is the package manager you wish your Mac shipped with. Once you set it up, Homebrew lets you install and update apps quickly and securely. It launched as a command-line interface, where you would type commands into the Terminal app on your Mac to install, update, or uninstall your apps. Recently, Homebrew launched its own GUI, which makes it easier than ever to use the service. Here are 10 Homebrew hacks that you should know, great for new and legacy users alike.

Once you update to Homebrew version 7.0.0 or newer, you'll notice that the service has a new GUI-enabled app for your Mac. You can launch it like any other app from the Applications folder, and use the interface to discover, install, update, and remove apps. The left pane has a few tabs that allow you to keep tabs on apps you've installed via Homebrew, updates available for those apps, fixes for issues with installation, and Homebrew settings. It also has an option called "Discover," which lets you search for apps available to install via Homebrew. Just use the search bar to look for your favorite apps, and if they show up, click the "Install" button. This will download that app to your Mac, and automatically complete the installation.

Homebrew has a "doctor" feature that lets you fix issues with the service. This can be anything from unsupported or deprecated apps, to issues with the Homebrew configuration itself. You can run this from the "Doctor" tab in the Homebrew GUI, or use the following command via Terminal:

The service will recommend some fixes, and you can run the suggested command in Terminal to solve the problem.

When you're using Homebrew via Terminal, you'll quickly notice that every action leaves you with a wall of text. This is great for those who want to track all those updates, or those who are roleplaying as characters from The Matrix, but not for everyone. If you want Homebrew to do its work quietly, just add the "-q" suffix to your commands. For example:

This will minimize the number of text updates on-screen, and leave you with a much cleaner Terminal. If you'd like to see more updates, you can replace "-q" with "-v" at the end of the command.

If you're not using Homebrew's GUI, it's easy to forget which apps you installed via Homebrew, and which ones are outside of it. To solve this, use the following command to show a list of all apps installed via Homebrew:

If you're like me, you've probably installed some apps via Homebrew, and downloaded a few others from the developers' websites. This means you can't update all your apps in one go, since some of them are not managed by Homebrew. You can fix this issue by adopting those apps into Homebrew. Use the following command to get this done:

brew install cask adopt APPNAME

As long as the apps are supported in Homebrew, this command will adopt them into the service. You can confirm the adoption by using the "brew list" command mentioned above.

When you install a lot of apps via Homebrew, it tends to create some clutter. Old versions of apps and cached downloads aren't always deleted immediately. If you're running short on space, you can try the following cleanup command to free up space without deleting apps:

This is one of the best features in Homebrew, and it works best right after a new version of macOS is released. This is when a flurry of app updates arrives to support the new operating system, and you can try this command to update all Homebrew apps in one go:

In case you just want to see which apps need an update, you can try this command:

The upgrade command is also listed under the "Upgrades" tab in the Homebrew GUI.

If you add the "dry run" flag to any install or update command, it will reveal a list of planned updates without commencing the installation. When you're dealing with command-line interfaces, "dry run" can be a useful way to preview changes before they take place, and to ensure that the correct app is being installed or updated. This is how you can use it:

If you're tired of typing long commands in Homebrew, you can set up aliases to minimize keystrokes. For instance, you can use "brew i" instead of "brew install" to update all Homebrew apps. Use this command to set this up:

Feel free to set up aliases for as many Homebrew commands as you like. The following command will list all the aliases you've set up:

To remove an alias, use this command:

Just remember to replace "i" with whichever alias you wish to remove.

If you don't want to update to the newest versions of certain apps, you can use the "pin" command to stop updates, and then "unpin" when you are ready to update again. This can be useful when an app you trust gets acquired by new owners who have yet to prove themselves, or if it adds new features you don't want, etc. Here's how to use it:

When you're ready to update it again, try this:

Note that you may also have to disable auto-updates from the app's interface separately because some apps just update themselves without confirmation.

title: The Boox Picco Is a Contender for My New Favorite Tiny E-Reader
description: I went hands-on with this competitor to the Xteink X4 Pro.
fullText:
Forget the Kindle Colorsoft—the release of the Xteink X4 last fall felt like the first truly interesting thing to happen to e-readers in years. A cheap, slightly clunky Chinese device with a 4.3-inch screen, its perfectly pocketable size (and a smart marketing gimmick—"You can attach it to the back of your phone with a magnet! Never mind that that isn't really a practical or sensible way to read!") quickly attracted an online cult following of tinkerers.

Xteink has since translated its viral social media success into mainstream awareness (including coverage in The New York Times), quickly releasing a flurry of new devices, including the Xteink X4 Pro, which brought familiar features like a front light and touchscreen into the mix. And the competition has definitely taken notice.

Boox, another Chinese company—albeit one that has been around for more than a decade—previously experienced a similar trajectory with the Palma, its own weirdly shaped e-reader. First released in 2023, that phone-shaped device appealed to readers who wanted something that was easier to carry than a full-sized Kindle and didn't tie them to the Amazon ecosystem. Yet even as the company prepares for the launch of the Palma 3 this fall, it's clearly not willing to let Xteink eat its lunch—hence the release of its own itty-bitty e-reader, the 3.97-inch Boox Picco.

First revealed in a surprise announcement back in July, the Picco is clearly modeled on Xteink's success—and with good reason, considering in many ways, the devices are identical by necessity. All e-reader screens are made by the same company, E-Ink, which means that all of these micro-readers—the Xteink X4, the X3, the X4 Pro, and, yes, the Picco—use the same screen with the same 480x800 resolution (though with more or fewer pixels per inch based on screen size, from 219ppi on the X4 Pro to 259ppi on the smaller X3). They also run on similar, simple ESP32 processors (though there's a bit more variation between models there) and make similar trade-offs, like abandoning onboard storage in favor of a microSD card slot. Like the X4 Pro, the Picco includes a temperature-adjustable front light and a touchscreen for navigation.

Firmware isn't even really a differentiating factor: Part of the reason for Xteink's early success was the fact that its simplicity made it easy to hack. No sooner had it found a following than a group of fans developed a custom firmware, called CrossPoint, that corrects most of the issues with Xteink's undeniably underbaked native operating system—there's even a website that makes flashing your reader with CrossPoint a matter of a single click. Early on, there was uncertainty about whether the Picco would run on Android like Boox's other devices, including the Palma. But no: Not only is Boox's device not a full-fledged Android device—it actually runs on a modified version of CrossPoint itself. Wild.

So, the components and firmware are darn similar on paper. How does the Boox Picco measure up in real life? Boox sent me a pre-release unit to test out, and after a day of messing around with it, I can report that it's pretty great. Do I like it more than the X4 Pro, its closest competitor in terms of features? I haven't quite decided.

Whatever their interior similarities, the Picco and the X4 Pro are pretty different at a glance. The Picco initially looks and feels much more refined, with a two-toned back panel and an aluminum frame and buttons that recall the iPhone 5, of all things. With a 3.97-inch display, it's slightly larger than the 3.7-inch Xteink X3 but smaller than the 4.3-inch X4 and X4 Pro. At this size, pixel density is around 235ppi, slightly sharper than the X4 Pro, though the difference is hard to spot when comparing them directly at a normal reading distance.

The Picco's 5.5mm thickness also sits between those devices (the X3 is 5.1mm thick, and the X4 Pro, 5.95mm). These differences are mostly inconsequential, though: Depending on your settings, all will display about the same number of words onscreen at the same time, and all will disappear easily into any pocket.

The Picco is also a lot lighter than the X4 Pro—58g versus 72g. It feels almost too light to me. Most of the weight difference is likely down to the fact that the Picco lacks the X4 Pro's internal magnets; the Boox device won't be able to snap into a magnetic case or clip to the back of your phone (though, again, I question why you'd want to do that). Whatever the reason, the lighter build makes the Picco feel slightly insubstantial to me.

Personally, I'm still trying to decide if I like the feel and form factor of the Picco—its straighter edges don't sit in my hand quite as comfortably as the Xteink devices, and I prefer the button placement on the X3 and X4 Pro that places forward and back page turn buttons on opposite sides of the device to the Picco's single right-side rocker button, which is small enough that I occasionally click to go back a page when I mean to go forward.

One unique touch: A switch on the left-hand side offers manual control over the front light (also adjustable in the on-screen menus), though you can also map it to turn on dark mode. It's tough to directly compare the front lights between the devices, as the firmware I'm running on the X4 Pro (CrossInk) overrides the native settings to allow more granularity in the brightness settings, but in terms of uniformity of the lighting and the cool/warm color balance, the devices seem identical.

Judging by the ongoing turmoil in the r/xteink subreddit, the biggest differentiating factor for many users will be the fact that the Picco charges and transfers files via a standard USB-C port, a feature Xteink has since dropped from all of its devices in favor of magnetic pogo pins, which require a separate cable or an adapter. Considering their battery life is measured in weeks even with daily reading, this isn't a big deal to me, but lots of people really care about it. Opting for USB-C was definitely a good call on Boox's end.

While the X4 Pro can easily be flashed to run CrossPoint, it currently ships with Xteink's own operating system, which is still a bit of a work in progress. Out of the box, the Picco is immediately much more usable, owing both to Boox's experience at building devices for a global market and to the fact that it's just a variant on CrossPoint, which most everyone who has used one of these wee readers already loves.

While the fun thing about CrossPoint is that there are hundreds of different forks that add or take away features to suit every user, the version that comes on the Picco is pretty darn good, all things considered. It displays your books well; it includes thoughtful options like a dark mode and the option to turn off the touchscreen; and it offers multiple options for getting files onto the device, including via connecting to a smartphone that's on the same wifi network, via the new BooxTile website/cloud app (not yet launched as of this writing), or by plugging it into your computer to act as an external USB drive. 

While the Picco does support Bluetooth connections, there are no menu options for it in the current firmware, which means you cannot (yet) connect to peripherals like the Boox Tappy remote page turner. There is, however, a menu of basic apps, including a simple pomodoro timer, some reading stats (including daily reading time and a graph charting your reading sessions over time), a to-do list, and a countdown timer. I can't imagine using any of these myself save the stats, but they're there if you want them.

There are limited options to customize things to your liking, including remapping the buttons to trigger different actions with a short or long press (like choosing to jump to the next chapter rather than the next page). You can also remap the touchscreen, though the options are limited to changing where to tap to change pages or open the in-book settings menu.

In terms of performance, the Picco feels just as fast as an X4 Pro running CrossInk, though the Pro has an ostensibly speedier ESP32-S3 processor (Boox hasn't specified exactly what processor the Picco uses). The Picco is generally faster when paging through a book quickly, suffering none of the momentary pauses for "indexing" that are common when reading on any Xteink device. It also seems to process and display cover art and embedded images much more quickly, despite the apparent lack of processing power.

It's not yet clear how much it will matter that the Picco has nicer firmware, however. Given it uses the same basic processor as the Xteink line (though one that is a bit less powerful than that in the X4 Pro, which has dual cores and 8MB of onboard RAM), it's very likely the Picco will also be flashable with custom software. In theory, this will mean that you will soon be able to pick and choose your own features from any number of options readily available online.

Whether you're interested in comparing the Picco to your Xteink device or are looking to buy your first tiny e-reader, you'll have to be patient: The Picco is not yet available for pre-order, directly from Boox or anywhere else. Rumors suggest a November release, though Boox has yet to provide a date. In the meantime, you can pick up the X4 Pro on Amazon. Whichever you choose, you'll be paying the same: Both devices come in at $99, around $50 less than the entry-level Kindle.

title: Bill Clinton mocks Trump's planned arch and questions Kennedy Center name fight
description:
Former President Clinton is knocking President Trump's plans for a triumphal arch and the efforts to put his name on the Kennedy Center, saying that global challenges would be more easily dealt with if leaders "didn't care as much about who got the credit."
The 42nd president delivered opening remarks at the opening of the annual Clinton Global Initiative meeting in New York on Tuesday. As he took to the lectern, Clinton quickly referenced Trump's recent announcement that plans for a massive arch bridging Washington and Virginia would incorporate a "top grade military complex" that would be used to store drones.
"I think it's important to take a few minutes to assess where we are now and the environment in which we are meeting," Clinton said. 
"I suppose I could take my entire allotted time to discuss the self-evident wisdom of building an Arc de Triomphe in Washington to hold all our drones," the former president said to laughs from the audience.
fullText:
Former President Clinton is knocking President Trump’s plans for a triumphal arch and the efforts to put his name on the Kennedy Center, saying that global challenges would be more easily dealt with if leaders “didn’t care as much about who got the credit.”

The 42nd president delivered opening remarks at the opening of the annual Clinton Global Initiative meeting in New York on Tuesday. As he took to the lectern, Clinton quickly referenced Trump’s recent announcement that plans for a massive arch bridging Washington and Virginia would incorporate a “top grade military complex” that would be used to store drones.

“I think it’s important to take a few minutes to assess where we are now and the environment in which we are meeting,” Clinton said.

“I suppose I could take my entire allotted time to discuss the self-evident wisdom of building an Arc de Triomphe in Washington to hold all our drones,” the former president said to laughs from the audience.

“Some of this stuff — it’s hard to make up,” he added.

“Over the course of a lifetime, there are only so many real opportunities to make decisions that we know will shape our personal history and the history of those we live with and care about for a long time to come. This is one of those moments,” he said, before mentioning the Kennedy Center board’s attempts to inscribe Trump’s name on the historic Washington building.

Last week, a federal judge blocked an effort by the Trump-picked board to add the president’s name to the institution and to rename its campus after Trump.

“I personally think that the way we’ve argued about what’s going on at the Kennedy Center and all that kind of stuff — I think we’ve been majoring in the minors,” Clinton said.

“You really think 100 years from now anybody’s going to care very much about whose name’s on what building?” he asked.

“Isn’t it more important what happens in the building? And what happens outside the building?” he continued.

“I feel so strongly — as I did 30 years ago-plus when I ran for president as a virtual child — that diversity is a positive thing, not a negative one.”

“That cooperation works better than conflict, and that we could actually deal with just about every challenge we face, if we didn’t care as much about who got the credit, and we made sure that we took care of the least of these,” Clinton, 80, said.

His remarks largely focused on dealing with the development of artificial intelligence and criticizing “zero-sum thinking” by the country’s political leaders.

“I believe that on the 250th anniversary of this country, we can’t have a politics driven by zero-sum thinking: In order for me to win, you have to lose,” he said.

“Nevertheless, I do understand why so many leaders around the world have chosen this zero-sum approach. Think how richly they have been rewarded for it in every sense of the word, and this payoff has been more apparent in the United States than any other country,” the former commander in chief said.

“Some days I can hardly believe what is happening in this country that I love so much. People in charge have created one set of rules for themselves and another set for everyone else,” Clinton said, without mentioning Trump by name.

“They’ve weaponized government to settle personal scores, prosecute enemies, stamp out free speech. They’ve even made the federal government a new profit center for themselves and their allies,” he said.

“That violates the spirit and letter of the Emoluments Clause of our Constitution.”

title: Israel FA comments on Hallgrimsson 'unacceptable' - Irish taoiseach Martin
description: Irish taoiseach Micheal Martin says comments made by the Israel Football Association about the Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson are "unacceptable".
fullText:
Irish taoiseach [prime minister] Micheal Martin said comments made by the Israel Football Association about the Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson are "unacceptable" and "should be withdrawn".

Israel's football governing body accused Hallgrimmson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity" regarding comments made last week when he said: "We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide. We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The teams are set to meet twice in the space of a week in the Nations League, with Israel's 'home' game in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday, with the return fixture also in a neutral venue of Backa Topola, Serbia on 4 October.

On Monday, the Israel FA posted a message on X, saying: "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way.

"Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach.

"We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, We're playing against the coach who embodies them."

While the Football Association of Ireland [FAI] did not respond, Martin did comment.

"They are unacceptable remarks and should be withdrawn," he told reporters in New York, where he is attending the UN General Assembly.

"We're very clear and I think [UN secretary-general] Antonio Guterres said it again this morning, he has never in his lifetime seen the level and scale of death and destruction as he witnessed in terms of the Israeli government's war on Gaza in the aftermath of the horrific Hamas attack preceding the war. Our manager is saying the exact same thing.

"Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious

Uefa rejected request to keep Republic of Ireland and Israel separate - FAI

There have been increasing calls in Ireland for a boycott of the fixtures, with a protest held at the Republic of Ireland team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

This followed an open letter by the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, signed by over 160 Irish sportspeople, urging the FAI to withdraw from the fixtures because of the situation in Gaza.

The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.

In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Israel has repeatedly denied that it has committed genocide, as well as war crimes and crimes against humanity. It says its military operations in Gaza have been conducted in self-defence and in accordance with international law.

title: Scarlets ready to 'come out fighting' with future at stake
description: Scarlets director of rugby Nigel Davies says talk about the organisation's long-term future has galvanised his squad before the new season starts this weekend.
fullText:
Scarlets director of rugby Nigel Davies says talk about the organisation's long-term future has galvanised his squad before the new season starts this weekend.

The Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) has outlined how it plans to cut from four men's professional teams to three by 2028, with Ospreys and Scarlets set to fight to be the side in west Wales.

The governing body says the decision will be made in time for the 2028-29 season, with one side in the capital, one in the east and one in the west.

WRU-owned Cardiff and Dragons, an independently backed business, are set to be given licences in the capital and east respectively.

That leaves Swansea-based Ospreys and Llanelli-based Scarlets to compete for the spot in the west, with a merger currently being ruled out.

"The situation has energised us," said Davies.

"It's typical Welsh, isn't it? You put us in the corner and we come out fighting."

WRU sticking to three-team plan - Reddin

Scarlets vow to remain at heart of west Wales

Scarlets chief Daniels dismisses Ospreys merger

The WRU has stated the process to decide the framework for the final decision will begin in December and finish before the end of the 2026-27 season.

So eyes will be on the results and attendances of Ospreys and Scarlets in this campaign, with the latter opening their United Rugby Championship (URC) campaign at home against Cardiff on Saturday night (19:45 BST).

"Performing on the field is the only way we're going to get our fans here," said Davies.

"We can't expect them to turn up unless we're performing, so we appreciate that, but we'd love them to all turn up on Saturday.

"It's a huge game which sets the stall out for the rest of the season."

Davies also says he realises the importance of local Welsh derbies which would be eroded if a team was culled.

"The rivalry is the best bit, isn't it?" said Davies.

"When you play against the Ospreys, Cardiff and Dragons, that's fantastic and long may that continue because that means so much to people.

"We don't get great crowds at the URC because of the logistics of the league, but in those events we do get good crowds.

"There's a need for that. People want to come and see those local derbies that we still have."

Davies says any final decision on the make-up of Welsh professional rugby should not be based on the 2026-27 campaign.

"You just can't look at a moment in time in Welsh rugby," said Davies.

"People will judge now because of the situation, so we realise there's a role and responsibility there as well for us to perform.

"We're not oblivious to that, but let's not forget this is more than just a moment in time."

Davies pointed to areas of strength that he believes benefit the Scarlets.

"There's a history and a legacy from this place," said Davies.

"We've also got this Parc y Scarlets facility, which nobody else has got, and we've got probably one of the strongest boards in Welsh rugby.

"So there's a lot of stuff that historically supports the Scarlets."

Davies also pointed to the development of players in west Wales.

"You've got to look at where the players historically come from," he said.

"Ourselves and the Ospreys have probably been the two most successful in developing rugby players into becoming Welsh internationals. You can't ignore that.

"There's a reason for that. These are strong communities with strong rugby heritage, strong colleges and strong schools that play rugby and develop those players.

"There are hotbeds within Welsh rugby. As the game is shrinking all the time, those hotbeds are key and vital."

Davies says the Welsh game, particularly the pathway, has been damaged in recent years

"Over the decades, we've eroded a lot of what was good about our game. I'm struggling to see what's left," said Davies.

"Our pathway doesn't identify talent now until 16, and it's difficult for a young rugby player or the parents of young rugby player to see a pathway for a player right now.

"I look at other areas of the union, and the liability of what they're doing, what they're trying to do and the lack of anything being driven at this moment in time."

Davies returned as interim director of rugby halfway through last season above head coach Dwayne Peel, with Scarlets eventually finishing 14th in the URC out of 16.

He was installed in a permanent role during the summer.

"I'm old enough now to have learned the fact that you never say never," said Davies.

"I was sort of planning my semi-retirement, but once the opportunity came, I had absolutely no hesitation.

"I know I've come back in a far stronger position in my experience and knowledge and the work I've done in other organisations."

Davies, 61, says he has learned new things since returning to Scarlets.

"One of the things for me personally is just culturally, the group, the generation, how you engage with this group is different to how it's been previously," said Davies.

"That's been quite a learning curve.

"It's a good thing. It brings diversity. We learn from each other and I've learned a lot of lessons.

"Some things I would have said previously probably aren't appropriate any more to say. I'm learning the triggers.

"It's been interesting and I've learned a lot myself over the last six months."

title: Wigan and Leigh face conduct probe, says RFL
description: Leigh Leopards and Wigan Warriors are issued letters to inform them there will be an independent investigation into their conduct over the past 12 months.
fullText:
Leigh Leopards and Wigan Warriors will face an independent investigation into their conduct over the past 12 months, the Rugby Football League has said.

The Super League play-off between the neighbouring clubs last October was overshadowed when Leopards owner Derek Beaumont said his side might boycott the fixture over a disagreement about their ticket allocation of 4,800.

The game ultimately went ahead as scheduled, with Wigan winning 18-6, but the Leopards submitted a complaint to the RFL the following week.

Wigan will host Wakefield in the play-off semi-final on Saturday and the Warriors released a statement last week to say whoever they played would receive an allocation of 5,000 tickets.

Trinity beat Leigh in their eliminator match, where a win for the opposition would have meant them progressing to face Wigan instead.

The RFL said in a statement: "The independent Rugby Football League and RL Commercial boards have issued a letter to both Leigh Leopards RLFC and Wigan Warriors RLFC advising them there will be an independent investigation into the conduct and actions of both clubs and the governing body in relation to matters extending over the last 12 months.

"The RFL and RL Commercial will not make any further comment until the investigation is complete."

BBC Sport has contacted both Leigh Leopards and Wigan Warriors for comment.

title: Five charged over football pitch hearse disorder
description: Five are charged over disorder which saw a hearse driven onto the pitch at Dunston UTC v Gateshead.
fullText:
Five men have been charged over the organisation of violent disorder after a funeral hearse was driven onto a football pitch.

Northumbria Police have been investigating a number of incidents from summer 2023, which are believed to be connected, including a hearse being driven onto the pitch at a Dunston UTC v Gateshead match at Dunston Football Club.

There were also reports of criminal damage across addresses in the Dunston and Byker areas, as well as a report of a stolen vehicle from the Durham area.

All five men who have been charged are due to appear at Sunderland and South Tyneside Magistrates' Court this week.

A hearse and a Subaru car were driven onto the pitch at the stadium on Wellington Road during half-time on 21 July 2023.

Those inside the hearse threw leaflets on to the pitch, before abandoning the vehicle and driving off in the Subaru - the match was later called off.

The leaflets included a number of personal allegations about two individuals.

The men due to appear in court are:

Carl Barron, 43, of Grange Villa, County Durham, who has been charged with two counts of conspiracy to commit criminal damage, conspiracy to make threats to kill and conspiracy to steal.

Ian Boddy, 44, previously of Bishop Auckland, County Durham, who has been charged with conspiracy to steal and participating in the activities of an organised crime group.

Darren Kay, 31, of Chester-Le-Street, County Durham, who has been charged with conspiracy to make threats to kill.

Graeme Rutherford, 54, of Birtley, Gateshead, who has been charged with two counts of conspiracy to commit criminal damage and conspiracy to make threats to kill.

John Wright, 42, of Tow Law, County Durham, who has been charged with two counts of conspiracy to commit criminal damage, conspiracy to make threats to kill and conspiracy to steal.

Det Ch Insp David Johnson, of Northumbria Police, said: "As ever, we would ask the public to refrain from any kind of speculation - both in the community and online - which could negatively impact the proceedings."

title: Pizza with Henry, captaining Brondby, and now a Scotland chance
description: From searching for pizza with Thierry Henry to leading a Danish Superliga side, Luis Binks has taken an unconventional route to the Scotland squad, writes Tom English.
fullText:
Every footballer has a story, but not many are quite as trippy as the one Luis Binks tells while sitting among the palm trees of La Manga, Scotland's training headquarters for a few days this week.

At 25, the Brondby centre-half and captain is pushing hard for a Scotland debut against Slovenia on Saturday, a spot in the heart of Sebastien Pocognoli's defence having opened up since Grant Hanley and John Souttar were jettisoned once the Belgian took over from Steve Clarke.

Binks, with a grandparent from Dunbar, is among the eight uncapped players in the new manager's squad.

That's a lot of new faces and a lot of new stories.

Binks talks about the early weeks of his time at Montreal Impact in the MLS; February to March, 2020. He was 18 and recalls: "I'd been at Tottenham since I was very young, but I just wanted to go and play first-team football.

"That was my biggest thing, to not get caught up in the whole youth system. I feel that if you get caught in that, it's not real football. I wanted to test myself."

Which brought him to Montreal where his manager was the great Thierry Henry.

"I'd signed in February and then we went into Covid lockdown in March," Binks explains. "I hadn't yet found an apartment. I was in one hotel and Thierry was in another. The one I was in was then shut down.

"He was staying at the Ritz on his own. They wanted to move me to a hotel by the airport and I didn't want to go because there was nothing there. It felt like prison, almost. One day I get a call from him, saying: 'Do you want to move to where I am? You can go on the other floor'."

The Ritz-Carlton is a five-star retreat with 129 rooms. Henry and Binks were the only residents.

"I'd go for runs in the morning and he'd be sat in the reception on his own. When I'd get back from the run, he'd still be sat there. I'd spend a few hours with him, just trying to pick his brains.

"I remember one night I was sat in my room just playing PlayStation and he rings me and goes, 'do you want to get a pizza?'. There's me and him driving around Montreal looking for a pizza. It's a bit surreal, but that was how it was.

"I'm saying it now like it's just anybody, but there's a big aura around him. I was nervous at the time, but I asked him who's the best defender he's played with and against and why and it was a good time.

"It's a bit of a blur now, but I always remember him talking about Sol Campbell and just saying what made him great and how I could improve as a defender.

"I owe a lot to him because he gave me my first chance in senior football."

McPake's 'colourful' journey from club-less to Scotland call-up in three years

Scotland call for Montgomery as Tierney & McLean drop out

Binks is a highly regarded centre-half who's been around. Tottenham, then Montreal and then spells at Bologna (where he befriended Aaron Hickey), Como, Coventry and now Brondby.

The Scotland call-up just continues his upward trajectory.

"I woke up every day with it on the top of my mind," he says of this training camp ahead of a journey to Ljubljana for the Nations League opener on Saturday.

"It's pretty cool. It's a bit of a weird feeling you don't get with club football. I'm buzzing to be here."

In the summer of 2025, Binks joined Brondby. "I wasn't really scared of the unknown," he says. "It was a chance for me to go and play again, hopefully play in Europe, fight for titles, cups. I want to win things. That was my whole reasoning."

He's the captain now, a role that sits well with him given that he spent so many years at Tottenham captaining pretty much every age-grade side he played for.

"People would say they could see that in me," he continues. "I'd only been at Brondby a year, so to be rewarded with that [captaincy] is a good sign. There's a lot of responsibility that goes with it.

"With Scotland, having been called up, the next thing is to try and play. It's my first camp, my first time meeting everyone, but deep down I want to leave a mark on this team."

title: The Wales captains looking to conquer England
description: Wales captains Dewi Lake and Jac Morgan prepare to make their Prem debuts for Gloucester after moving from Ospreys.
fullText:
You might argue that for Welsh rugby to lose one Wales captain to an English club was unfortunate but two on the same day was just careless.

That is what happened in December 2025 when flanker Jac Morgan and hooker Dewi Lake announced they were leaving Ospreys for Gloucester for the 2026-27 season.

A two-for-one deal for the English club, who are investing in the Welsh duo to help turn their fortunes around.

Now the pair are preparing to make their Prem debuts against Exeter this Saturday.

Lake has been unveiled as the new Gloucester captain with Morgan as one of his deputies, demonstrating the favourable impression the pair have already made.

BBC Sport Wales caught up with them at their new Kingsholm home to talk about their early Gloucester experiences, leaving Ospreys and Welsh rugby politics behind and forgetting they are speaking Welsh in their new English environment.

Why are Wales' captains leaving for England?

Singleton hopes for return after heart attack

Losing Gloucester captaincy was 'brutal' - Ludlow

The duo have been almost inseparable since meeting a decade ago and were chosen as co-captains for the 2023 World Cup by former Wales coach Warren Gatland.

Lake is 27 and Morgan 26, with only eight months separating them.

Where one is, the other is never far behind, with Lake and Morgan having developed an almost telepathic understanding. They do not quite finish each other's sentences. But it is not far off.

The pair say they did not speak to each other about signing for Gloucester but fate has ensured they stay together in the next chapter of their rugby story.

"I am incredibly happy we got to land at the same club together," said Lake.

"We have come up together and spent 10 years day in, day out.

"He's an incredible friend off the field, but on the field also an incredible leader and player.

"Even the first day at Gloucester, we texted each other and said we'll meet at half past seven in the car park because neither of us wanted to go in on our own.

"To be able to get to see him day in day out and still spend time with him is incredible. I feel the bond we've created is really strong."

Lake described Gloucester as not too dissimilar to life in Wales, helped by a strong Welsh contingent of Max Llewellyn, Freddie Thomas, Josh Hathaway and Deian Gwynne who are already at Kingsholm.

Morgan agreed, saying: "It's been like a home from home. It's great to have a couple of fellow Welshmen here."

Not just fellow Welshmen but Welsh speakers, with Gwynne and Llewellyn comfortably conversing in their native language.

"A lot of us are speaking Welsh to each other when we're in the building," said Morgan.

"So it's been great to be able to do that. It's hard sometimes when you know someone can speak Welsh, it's hard to speak English to them!"

Lake added: "Jac and I rarely speak English to each other.

"We've got to catch ourselves and stop ourselves sometimes when other people are involved in conversations as well.

"In our first week we caught ourselves talking Welsh to each other at the breakfast table.

"We apologised and were forgetting we're not in Wales anymore, but we still speak Welsh to each other where we can."

The duo are grateful the infamous Gloucester "milk challenge" initiation stopped before they joined.

New players used to have to finish eight pints of milk within a time limit of about 20 minutes without being sick.

The penalty for being sick or not finishing the challenge in time was having their head shaved.

"It's gone, thankfully," said Lake.

"Jac and I spent the full summer on ChatGPT with pictures of ourselves bald just to start preparing ourselves."

It has been replaced by a more physical "shed challenge" that includes running up and down steps with sandbags and flipping tyres.

"Being here at Gloucester has been class so far," said Lake.

"The boys and coaches have been welcoming, it feels like a place where I'm able to get better, learn a lot and test my game in a new league.

"I wanted to challenge myself and be uncomfortable, if you like, in a new environment.

"That's the reason why I decided to make the move and I'm sure Jac feels the same."

Morgan says Gloucester being a traditional rugby city and community was a draw.

"A lot of people have been stopping us in the street and saying welcome to Gloucester," said Morgan.

"You can see how much this club means for the city and you sense the history.

"A lot of the boys mentioned 'the Shed' [Kingsholm stand], so it'll hopefully be a great experience to be able to play in front of the home crowd.

"We want to get a few more wins this year, do better than last year and see where it goes."

Morgan has also drawn on previous Welsh legends at Gloucester with Tomos Williams, James Hook and Richard Hibbard having previously played at Kingsholm.

"There's a lot of Welsh who have played here in the past and they're part of the history," said Morgan.

"There's a photo of Hibs [Hibbard] up in the corridors there, so it's good being able to see that.

"You speak to a lot of the past players about their experiences and Gloucester loved having them at the club."

Lake and Morgan join a sizeable Welsh contingent in English club rugby this season alongside the likes of Aaron Wainwright, Dafydd Jenkins, Rhys Carre, Nicky Smith, Tomas Francis, Tomos Williams and Louis Rees-Zammit.

Despite the excitement of their new life, Morgan and Lake are sad to leave Ospreys behind.

"We're both thankful of everything the Ospreys have given us over the last few years and the bonds we created with players and coaches," said Morgan.

"Probably the hardest part was leaving the people and you've got best mates back at home.

"We're still in contact with everybody but the lack of day-to-day contact is probably one of the hardest things to leave."

That passion includes paying to watch their old side.

"We still come in Mondays and the first thing we talk about is the Ospreys score on the weekend," said Lake.

"We both paid £5 the other night to watch them play against Coventry in a pre-season game.

"So the love for the club and people is still there with both of us and will not go away.

"It was a tough decision to leave, it was always going to be. Ospreys did everything for us, gave us an opportunity and platform and the chance to represent our country."

One thing they do not miss is the Welsh rugby politics, with Lake and Morgan signing for Gloucester at a time of uncertainty over whether Ospreys would survive beyond last season.

"The off-the-field stuff going on in background was tough to deal with sometimes," said Lake.

"It's nice to get away from it sometimes. It's one less thing to think about when you're playing here. It's easier for us to be here and not think of it.

"Over the last year or two, it's kind of dictated a lot that's gone on at the Ospreys, in terms of stuff we've had to do away from training and representing that region.

"It'll never be something we don't think about because we've still got friends there that will be affected by what is going on.

"We will try and catch up with the boys back home and still worry about them."

Since Morgan and Lake announced their Gloucester move, Ospreys have been given a stay of execution for at least two seasons.

But one of Ospreys or Scarlets are set to disappear by 2028 with a professional side in the west being cut by the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU).

"We don't have to deal with it but we still love the club and want Ospreys to be safe," said Lake.

"That's something we speak of and think about often."

Ospreys say WRU plan to cut team is wrong

WRU sticking to three-team plan - Reddin

Resilient Ospreys players need certainty - Jones

Lake and Morgan are set to return to Wales for the Nations Championship in November.

A victory in the summer against Fiji was followed by away defeats against Argentina and South Africa, with home games against Japan, New Zealand and Australia to follow in the autumn.

Reflecting on the summer campaign, Lake said: "It was a mixed bag. The Argentina game was probably the most disappointing.

"We had enough talent in our tank to beat that team but we didn't make them work too hard and we let ourselves down.

"I still think it's a positive summer in terms of where we've been, compared to where we are now.

"We can see the the growth and the fact we're talking about we should have beaten Argentina.

"We wouldn't have been saying that two years ago."

A World Cup in Australia is on the horizon in a year's time but firstly the new life in Gloucester awaits. One Lake and Morgan will enjoy together.

title: Menzies upsets Van Veen to win second title of year
description: Scotland's Cameron Menzies celebrates his second tournament win of the year after beating Gian van Veen to the Players Championship 29 title in Den Bosch.
fullText:
Scotland's Cameron Menzies is celebrating his second tournament win of the year after beating Gian van Veen to the Players Championship 29 title in Den Bosch.

Menzies raced into a 5-0 lead against the home favourite, who is third in the PDC rankings, before prevailing 8-4.

"To go and win another ProTour is awesome. I'm so happy," said Menzies.

"This is my fifth year on the tour and I've won four ProTours. That's not bad I suppose.

"My aim is to make a good life for myself. That's the aim that I think is achievable, but winning a major and having a good run at the World Championship would be amazing.

"I've put more effort in this year than I ever have because I nearly lost it all and I'm grateful to be in this position."

Menzies, ranked 26th, had considered quitting darts earlier this year after damaging his hand while angrily punching a drinks table following a first-round exit at the World Championship.

In July, the Scot was victorious at Players Championship 23 in Leicester.

Later that month, Menzies beat world number two Luke Humphries in the first round of the World Matchplay, only to fall ill in his next match.

En route to the final in Den Bosch, he got past Kevin Doets, Jeffrey de Graaf, Wessel Nijman, Benjamin Pratnemer, Jim Long and Nick Kenny.

title: Lopez ordered to defend world title against Britain's Catterall
description: Briton Jack Catterall is one step closer to a second world title shot, having lost his previous one in 2022.
fullText:
Teofimo Lopez has been ordered to defend his WBA world title against Briton Jack Catterall.

Lopez became the WBA 'super' welterweight champion with a points win over Rolando Romero last month.

Catterall, 33, is Lopez's mandatory challenger but the American has been campaigning to fight WBC champion Ryan Garcia in a unification bout instead.

The WBA has now announced they expect Lopez to fight Catterall next, and the two parties have until 22 October to reach an agreement or there will be a purse bid.

Catterall became the number one challenger and WBA 'regular' title-holder after beating Shakhram Giyasov in May.

He acknowledged the WBA's ruling on X, saying: "Hi Teofimo Lopez."

The Chorley native last fought for a world title in 2022 when he was controversially beaten by then undisputed light-welterweight champion Josh Taylor.

Lopez, a three-weight world champion, could withdraw from negotiations and relinquish his world title, which may lead to Catterall being upgraded to world champion.

Lopez attended the Garcia v Conor Benn fight week in Las Vegas earlier this month and was stopped from entering the ring after Garcia's quick win.

Catterall has just two defeats on his record - to Taylor and American Arnold Barboza Jr - with 33 wins and 14 stoppages.

Lopez, 29, also has two losses during his career, a 2021 points loss to George Kambosos Jr and more recently a decision defeat by Shakur Stevenson in January.

title: Record prize fund for 2028 European Championships
description: The European Athletics Championships will have a total record prize fund worth £3m when it takes place in Poland in 2028.
fullText:
The European Athletics Championships in 2028 will offer a record prize fund worth about £3m when they are staged in Silesia, Poland.

Prize money will be awarded to athletes finishing in the top eight across all 50 events.

Gold medal winners will earn 30,000 euros (£25,720), while silver and bronze medallists will receive 15,000 euros (£12,860) and 10,000 euros (£8,573) respectively.

Athletes finishing fourth to eighth across the 50 disciplines will receive awards of 5,000, 4,000, 3,000, 2,000 and 1,000 euros respectively.

European Athletics has restructured the way in which prize money is awarded, ensuring athletes finishing in the top eight in every discipline receive financial recognition.

The prize fund on offer at the last championships, held in Birmingham in August of this year, did not involve a standard payout for every medal position.

Instead, a total pot of 500,000 euros (£428,000) was split equally between the top 10 performances across 10 categories - five for men and five for women - determined by the World Athletics scoring tables.

Great Britain and Northern Ireland won 19 medals in Birmingham, including nine golds.

But none of those gold medal performances earned one of the 50,000 euro 'Gold Crown' bonuses awarded by the organisers.

The significant increase in money for the European Championships reflects how elite athletes' on-track earning potential is growing.

World Athletics recently provided what it described as "the richest prize pot in the history of the sport", with $10m (£7.4m) put up for its new three-day Ultimate Championship event in Budapest.

Each individual event winner received $150,000 (£110,000).

How did the first Ultimate Championship go?

How the race they said women couldn't run took centre stage

With athletes carefully planning their seasons, championships may need to offer substantial incentives to ensure strong fields.

There will be another Ultimate Championship in 2028, plus the Los Angeles Olympics and a Diamond League season.

The European Championships will take place in early June, starting six weeks before the Olympics get under way.

European Athletics said its revised structure for 2028 ensures every discipline is treated equally and there will now be "due recognition" given not only to medal winners but to all athletes reaching the top eight.

The governing body's chief executive, Christian Milz, said the decision "demonstrates our commitment" to competitors who are "at the heart of our sport".

"We are seeing European athletes produce extraordinary performances and capture the imagination of audiences around the world," he said.

"It is important that we continue to find meaningful ways to recognise and support them, and this record prize fund is a significant step in that direction."

title: I was close to joining Liverpool in 2016 - Mbappe
description: Kylian Mbappe says his mum was a "big fan" of Jurgen Klopp and wanted her son to move to Merseyside.
fullText:
Kylian Mbappe has revealed how "close" he came to joining Liverpool in 2016, saying he went against the advice of his mother who "fell in love" with Anfield.

The France and Real Madrid striker said the Reds tried to sign him at 18, while he was playing for Monaco in Ligue 1.

Former Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp said the club laid on a private jet and food for Mbappe and his family in an attempt to sign him, before he eventually joined Paris St-Germain.

Speaking to the Athletic, Mbappe said his mum was a "big fan" of Klopp and wanted her son to move to Merseyside.

"I was close to [joining] Liverpool. The favourite destination for my mum was Liverpool. She wanted me to go there," he said.

"I didn't listen because I wanted to play in my city, Paris. I didn't want to leave my country before I was someone.

"But yes, my mum was always saying, 'Liverpool - you're going to be there, playing at Anfield, it's going to be insane for you'."

Mbappe, now 27, said his mother went out to Liverpool for the "first step" of the negotiation.

"She went to the city, the stadium, she met the people. She was like, 'it's a wonderful club, everybody's so kind, it's a family club, a big club', said Mbappe.

"She went to Anfield and fell in love with it. She watched a few games alone, to feel the atmosphere, because she wanted to imagine me in this stadium."

Klopp, who spoke about the possible move on Magenta TV as a pundit at the 2026 World Cup, explained how a flight was taken from Blackpool to Nice in France, where "the entire Mbappe family boarded a private jet with five rooms or something".

"We really went all out. Then we flew around in a circle, talked with the family, ate good food," Klopp said.

He said they had not wanted to be seen having talks - but the meeting proved fruitless.

"We flew in a circle. It was fantastic. And then he went to Paris," Klopp added.

"It's a funny story," said Mbappe.

"But in the end, I took the decision to go to PSG because for me, born and raised in Paris, there was no better feeling than to show I could be a star in my hometown."

Mbappe later joined PSG on loan, in a deal including an option for the move to become permanent for 180m euros (£165.7m). He went on to spend seven years in Paris, becoming the club's record scorer before leaving for Real Madrid in 2024.

title: Banned British player's £15m lawsuit against WTA dismissed
description: British player Tara Moore's legal bid for £15m in damages over a doping case which led to her being banned for four years is dismissed.
fullText:
British doubles player Tara Moore's legal bid for £15m ($20m) in damages from the Women's Tennis Association - over a doping case which led to her being banned for four years - has been dismissed by a United States court.

Moore, 34, argued the WTA - the governing body of the women's tour - failed to warn players about the risk of eating contaminated meat at a tournament held in Colombia.

But the United States District Court in New York has dismissed Moore's motion and directed to "close this matter".

Moore, who has always denied intentionally doping, told BBC Sport after the ruling that the case has been a "nightmare".

"It just shows how broken the anti-doping system is in tennis," Moore said.

Keothavong 'can't fault' GB after BJK Cup loss to Czechs

GB dominate Ecuador to reach Davis Cup Finals

In April 2022, Moore tested positive for nandrolone and boldenone at a WTA 250 event in Bogota, with an independent tribunal ruling in December 2023 that contaminated meat was the source.

Moore, who was Britain's leading women's doubles player at the time of the failed test, was found to bear "no fault or negligence", but the International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) appealed against the decision.

Last year, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) ruled in favour of the ITIA and Moore was banned until 2028.

Moore then initiated proceedings with the American Arbitration Association, in which she claimed the WTA's "failure to warn against eating meat in Colombia was a direct cause of her positive test result and the harm that followed".

The arbitrator supported the ruling made by Cas and dismissed the case against the WTA.

In response, Moore filed a motion against the decision at the United States District Court in New York.

Moore, who was ranked a career-high 77th in the world in 2022, claimed she was denied a fair hearing by the arbitrator.

The motion detailed how Moore was seeking "no less than $20m in compensatory damages" after claiming the WTA "stayed silent in the face of a known and specific danger and then shifted the blame for its own negligence" to the player.

On Friday, United States district judge Andrew Carter found Moore's challenge was "not justified" on a legal basis.

The WTA and ITIA have been approached for comment.

title: Who will start for England at Euro 2028? BBC Sport's predictions
description: As England prepare to face world champions Spain on Saturday, BBC Sport's experts predict who will be starting for the Three Lions at Euro 2028.
fullText:
Less than two months after Spain were celebrating their World Cup triumph, the next major tournament cycle begins.

From 9 June 2028, the European Championship will be hosted by England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland - and the path to the finals starts now.

England host Spain on Saturday in their Nations League opener and, while the competition doesn't offer a direct qualification route, it does provide a secondary route for teams who don't qualify automatically.

Despite being co-hosts of Euro 2028, Thomas Tuchel's men are not guaranteed a spot in the tournament - with all hosts having to earn their place.

But, assuming England will qualify for the tournament, who do you think will be in the side for the opener in the summer of 2028?

We have asked some BBC Sport experts for their predictions and want you to pick your team using the selector at the bottom of the page.

Will England boss Tuchel 'embrace the chaos'?

Just a couple of changes from the World Cup.

Jordan Pickford will be 34 by the time Euro 2028 starts so no problem there for goalkeeper, although James Trafford will mount a serious challenge.

I would pick Trent Alexander-Arnold at right-back but I am still not convinced Tuchel trusts him even though he has handed him an England recall.

On that basis I have selected Tino Livramento, if he can stay fit, although I still hope Tuchel puts doubts about Alexander-Arnold out of his mind.

If Everton's Jarrad Branthwaite can steer clear of injury – if – then I think Tuchel could partner him with Marc Guehi in the centre of defence, with Nico O'Reilly staying on the left.

Personal preference persuades me to pick Adam Wharton ahead of Elliot Anderson – who I do rate very highly – with Declan Rice a no-brainer. Tuchel could go either way but I believe Wharton can win that fight between now and then, despite missing out on that final squad.

Of course there will be claims for Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and even Morgan Gibbs-White, but Jude Bellingham ended any arguments, such as they were, about his class and place in the team with a brilliant World Cup. Where would you play them?

I'm banking on Harry Kane having one more major tournament in him, even though he will be pushing 35 – and let's face it, who else is there?

Bukayo Saka is another certain pick in my opinion, but I believe Liverpool's Rio Ngumoha will develop as such a rate he will be an England regular by 2028, so he gets the nod on the left.

This is largely the same team that was viewed as England's first choice at the World Cup, apart from Morgan Rogers (although I think it will be a close call between him and Anthony Gordon).

It's a team packed with players who will all be in their peak years and at the moment, it's hard to see anyone coming out of the team in the next two years.

On the bench, however, England will have some fresh options with the likes of Rio Ngumoha, Alex Scott, Lewis Miley and even Max Dowman likely to be pushing for a spot in the squad.

But when you consider that England have reached a World Cup semi-final and a European Championship final in the past two years it does suggest that this group of players are close and there is nothing there to be ripped up.

And the fact England would be playing on home soil has to increase their chances of finally getting the job done.

I would not be surprised to see James Trafford and Dean Henderson given opportunities in goal but it may be that by the tournament it is still his experience that gives Jordan Pickford the edge. Maybe it would be different if the other two were playing for teams challenging for the major honours.

I expect Tino Livramento, Lewis Hall and Ben White to be staking a claim in the full-back positions.

And obviously Morgan Rogers, Cole Palmer, perhaps Morgan Gibbs-White and maybe by then Max Dowman will be close to the starting line-up. But I don't think the 11 I've named above would be too far away from the reality.

When Euro 2028 kicks off on 9 June in two years' time, England captain Harry Kane will be 34 years and 317 days old and knowing his levels of desire, he will be determined to lead England for that tournament on home soil.

Barring injury then I can see him still leading the line for his country and I would also back Jordan Pickford still to be in goal too.

In fact if you look at the current squad then it's hard to see who would not be around as this group of players continue to grow together for England. Ezri Konsa would be the only other 30-something which is why my starting XI has a very familiar feel to it.

I would back Max Dowman to be part of the England squad for 2028 but in terms of a starter my only area of uncertainty is at right-back.

There have been nine different players to have started in that position since September 2024.

I wouldn't rule out Archie Gray to force his way into contention. Like Nico O'Reilly I could see another midfielder adapting into that position on the right. I saw him play there as Spurs captain recently and he has the quality, temperament and leadership qualities to step up to senior international level.

Starting with the goalkeeper, I think Jordan Pickford will still be the England number one but James Trafford after a couple more seasons of Premier League football will be pushing him close.

It was a very tight call for Adam Wharton or Myles Lewis-Skelly in the middle of the pitch but with Tuchel still likely to be in charge I think he will go for the more physical Lewis-Skelly as his number six.

Jarrad Branthwaite could be the key physical centre-back and as a left footer will bring balance to the defence but this pick could also go to Levi Colwill.

Max Dowman will be 18 years old by the time the next Euros comes around and will likely be in the squad and could be challenging Saka while Brian Madjo looks to be the next bright natural number nine and could be Kane's understudy for this tournament.

You have seen what the BBC experts think, but who do you reckon will start for England at Euro 2028?

title: Cyclist who dressed as man to avoid Taliban wins silver medal
description: Afghan cyclist Fariba Hashimi wins silver in the women's road race at the Asian Games, having fled oppression in her home country to pursue a sporting dream.
fullText:
A female cyclist from Afghanistan who previously disguised herself as a man when chasing a career in the sport has won a silver medal at the Asian Games.

Fariba Hashimi fled her country after the Taliban returned to power in 2021.

She says she trained in disguise out of necessity before then in an effort to avoid being attacked, in a country where women's rights are heavily restricted.

She earned her medal in the women's road race near Nagoya in Japan on Tuesday.

The 23-year-old's achievement follows her seventh-place finish in the women's individual time trial on Sunday.

Describing her medal as "something special", Hashimi hopes it can inspire other women in Afghanistan to follow their dreams.

"I was born inside a country where the women who dream are getting attacked, and I'm really happy that I have fought against that," she said.

"I hope that the next generation will come here and represent their country without any fear."

Banned from football at home, Afghan women's team reunite 8,000 miles away

King meets women's cricket team that is not allowed to exist

Hashimi followed her sister Yulduz, also an international cyclist, into the sport at the age of 15, despite danger in their home province of Faryab.

"I always dressed as a man to go to training, wearing two or three different masks so ‌people ⁠would not recognise or attack me," Hashimi previously told Reuters., external

Hashimi said she would have to avoid stones being thrown at her whilst riding her bike.

Hashimi now lives and trains in Italy thanks to help from the Italian former world champion Alessandra Cappellotto.

Looking back at life in Afghanistan, Hashimi said the Taliban "took away our freedom".

"This silver medal can show a lot of resilience from Afghan women, and I'm really happy," she said.

"I'm not alone, I know that behind me millions of women, from many countries, have the same dream and they are standing with me."

Hashimi and her sister competed at the 2024 Paris Olympics and are now setting their sights on the 2028 Los Angeles Games.

"I never want to give up," Hashimi said, "and hopefully we can see [what can happen] again in Los Angeles."
